claims.text: As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of 786 MPa.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa and a terminal strain of 13.5%.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has relatively coarse grains and limited tensile ductility.
Hot rolling followed by a controlled subrecrystallization anneal will refine the grains of HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will produce a bimodal distribution of fine and retained coarse grains.
Grain refinement will increase total grain-boundary area.
The refined, bimodal structure will promote more homogeneous accumulation and distribution of dislocations.
Fine grains and microstructural heterogeneity will provide additional barriers to dislocation motion and help maintain high strength.
The processed microstructure will activate additional strain-hardening mechanisms.
Greater strain hardening will delay tensile necking and increase uniform elongation.
The treatment could raise uniform tensile elongation from a stated 13.5% baseline to above 20%.
The treatment will limit the reduction in yield strength to less than 10% relative to the as-cast state.
The processed alloy will retain impact-triggered energetic performance comparable to the as-cast alloy.
The tensile improvement is intended to apply at room temperature.
The hypothesis applies at strain rates described only as similar to conventional rolling operations.
Energetic performance should be tested under conditions comparable to thin-steel-target penetration.
Excessive annealing or processing could cause grain overgrowth or softening and thereby reduce strength.
Over-processing could embrittle the alloy or alter its phase balance and impact energy release.
Rolling and heat treatment produced a fine-grained CoCrNiV alloy with 1060 MPa yield strength and 24.1% uniform elongation.
A heterogeneous Fe35Ni29Co21Al12Ta3 microstructure containing L12 nanoprecipitates and B2 microparticles achieved 1.8 GPa yield strength and 25% uniform elongation.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies hot rolling, but the conditions state that processing and subsequent tensile testing occur at room temperature. Hot rolling necessarily occurs at elevated temperature, so processing temperature is internally inconsistent.

The 13.5% value is introduced as terminal strain alongside compressive properties, but it is later treated as the baseline uniform tensile elongation. Terminal compressive strain and uniform tensile elongation are not interchangeable.
